title: Dependency injection and IoC
idea: Dependency injection (DI) means a class receives the objects it needs instead of creating them; inversion of control (IoC) means something outside the class decides and wires them.

analogy.text: A film crew does not hire its own camera. The production office books one and delivers it; the crew only says it needs a camera.
analogy.breaks: Offices pick once per film; a container can rebuild objects on demand.

points: A class declares what it needs as constructor parameters typed by interfaces.
One composition root, often `main`, creates concrete objects and passes them in.
Swapping an implementation, or a test fake, needs no edit to the class.
An IoC container such as Spring automates the wiring from registered recipes.

hero.title: Who calls new, and who just uses

steps.caption: `OrderService` holds a `private final Notifier`. It never writes `new` for one.
`main` is the composition root. It creates a `ConsoleNotifier` first.
It passes that object into the `OrderService` constructor. That is constructor injection.
`place` calls `notifier.send`. The service sees only the `Notifier` role.
For a test, `main` injects a `RecordingNotifier` instead. No line of `OrderService` changes.
The fake records the call, so a check can read what was sent.
Control is inverted: the class asks for help, and the outside decides which help arrives.

code.title: Constructor injection
code.caption: One service, two notifiers, chosen by `main`. The service code is identical in both runs.

walk.text: The role: an interface with one method, named for what it does.
The dependency is a `private final` field set only by the constructor.
The service uses the role and never names a concrete class.
The composition root picks the real notifier for normal use.
The same service gets a recording fake, which a test can inspect.

code.title: A tiny IoC container
code.caption: A container holds recipes and builds each object once, then reuses it. Spring does the same wiring at scale, though by default it builds singletons at startup.

walk.text: `register` stores a recipe: a function that builds the type from the container.
`get` builds on first request, keeps the instance, and returns it after that.
The `Greeter` recipe asks the container for its `Clock`; it never calls `new FixedClock`.
The caller asks for a ready `Greeter`; the container resolved the whole graph.
`Greeter` is plain constructor injection; it works with or without a container.

pitfalls: Do not call `new` for a collaborator inside a class you want to test or swap.
Prefer constructor injection over setter or field injection; it keeps fields `final` and objects complete.
Do not pass the container itself into business classes; that hides their real dependencies.

quiz.q: Using `Container` above, what does this print?
quiz.why: Recipes run only when `get` is called, and both are registered by then. The clock says 15, which is not below 12, so it says Hello.

takeaway: Ask for dependencies through the constructor; let one outside place wire them.
